393.title: The quail and the hawk
393.hook: a quail safe in its own field is caught when it strays (SN 47.6)
393.howItsDone: In many Buddhist communities, mindfulness is described as a practitioner's own ground or home base, returned to through the day; monastics often keep simple routines and guard the senses when they go into town as a way of staying in that range.

segments.voice: Yesterday: six animals, the six senses, tied to one steady post. The post holds.

A hawk drops out of the sky and comes up with a quail in its claws. And the quail, being carried off, starts talking. Not begging. Scolding itself. This is my own fault, it says. I wandered out of my own range into somebody else's. If I'd stayed in my home ground, the ground my mother and father knew, this hawk would be no match for me. The hawk, apparently amused, asks: and where is this home ground of yours? A plowed field, says the quail, covered with clods of earth.
screen: `A QUAIL IN THE HAWK'S CLAWS.` → `I LEFT MY OWN GROUND.` → `A PLOWED FIELD, FULL OF CLODS.`

segments.voice: This is SN 47.6, in the Connected Discourses on mindfulness. The hawk, proud of its strength, lets the quail go. Fine, it says. Go home. Even there you won't escape me. The quail flies back to its plowed field, climbs onto a big clod of earth, and calls up: come and get me now, hawk. The hawk folds its wings and dives at full speed. The quail watches it come, and at the last moment slips down behind the clod. The hawk hits the earth breast first. Then the Buddha explains. Don't wander outside your own range, monks, into the range of others. In others' ground, Mara, the tempter, gets his chance. Others' range is the five cords of sense pleasure: sights, sounds, smells, tastes and touches that pull at desire. Your own range, the ground your fathers knew, is the four foundations of mindfulness: the body, feelings, the mind, and the patterns of experience. The quail isn't stronger than the hawk. It simply knows its ground, every furrow, every clod. Safety in this story isn't power; it's familiarity. And the text's word for range is gocara, a pasture, the ground a grazing animal knows by heart. Mindfulness isn't a fortress you build. It's a field you know so well you can disappear into it. The hawk doesn't stop being a hawk. What changes is where the quail is standing when one comes.
screen: `THE HAWK LETS THE QUAIL GO.` · `A CLOD IN A PLOWED FIELD.` · `YOUR RANGE: THE FOUR FOUNDATIONS.` · `GOCARA — A PASTURE KNOWN BY HEART.` · then, large: `YOUR OWN GROUND.`

segments.voice: Make your field small, the breath and the body sitting, and get to know its clods: where the breath touches first, where the body is heavy. When a thought flies off toward someone else's field, a plan, a worry, a screen, notice that you've left, and come back to one clod you know: one breath, one point of contact.
Gocara, range or pasture. Safety isn't strength; it's staying in your own range, the four foundations of mindfulness.
Your line: your own ground. The quail wins by knowing its field, not by being strong. Till tomorrow.

394.title: The monkey and the pitch
394.hook: a monkey caught in a hunter's sticky pitch by grabbing with every limb (SN 47.7)
394.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often use this simile to describe how grasping compounds itself; many practitioners work with it by pausing to notice an urge before acting on it, in meditation and in daily life.

segments.voice: Yesterday: gocara, the quail's plowed field. Your own ground is the four foundations of mindfulness.

In the Buddha's story, hunters in the Himalaya have a trick for catching monkeys. No net. No arrow. Just a smear of sticky pitch along the trails where monkeys travel. A wise monkey sees it and keeps going. A curious one touches it with one paw. Stuck. So it uses the other paw to pull the first one free. Stuck. Then a foot. Then the other foot. Then, out of ideas, it tries its mouth.
screen: `PITCH ON THE MONKEY TRAIL.` → `ONE PAW. THEN THE OTHER.` → `THEN THE FEET. THEN THE MOUTH.`

segments.voice: This is SN 47.7, right next to the quail. The Buddha describes three kinds of mountain country: rugged places where neither monkeys nor people go, places where monkeys go but people don't, and even, pleasant places where both go. In that third kind, hunters lay pitch along the trails. The foolish monkey, stuck at five points, lies there crying out, and the hunter does with it as he pleases. The lesson matches the quail's: keep to your own range, the four foundations of mindfulness. The range of others is the five cords of sense pleasure. But this picture adds something. The quail story is about where you are. The monkey story is about how you get stuck: by trying to get unstuck the same way you got stuck. Every limb that grabs to free the first gets caught too. An argument you try to win with one more message. A craving you try to settle with one more taste. A worry you try to think your way out of. The pitch is laid where life is pleasant; that's the point of putting it there. Mindfulness is the pause before the second paw: seeing the pitch as pitch. The text doesn't call the monkey wicked or the forest evil. The wise monkey sees the pitch and walks around it. That closes six days on right mindfulness: remembering to notice, the gatekeeper, the bowl of oil, the six animals and their post, the quail's own ground, and the monkey.

segments.voice: Look for one sticky place, a thought you keep returning to, a sound you keep resisting, and notice the second paw: the urge to fix it or push it away right now. Let your hands rest open on your knees and just watch the pull; it may stay, and you're only learning where the pitch is.
Makkata, monkey. The trap that holds you tighter the more you grab to get free.
Your line: don't grab the pitch. Grabbing to get free only sticks you tighter. Day three hundred ninety-four, done.

395.title: Right concentration
395.hook: the mind gathered and unified, in the four jhanas (MN 141)
395.howItsDone: Buddhists across schools train concentration in meditation, often on the breath; in Theravada communities it is commonly taught as calm (samatha) alongside insight (vipassana), and Zen and Tibetan schools have their own methods for steadying the mind.

segments.voice: Yesterday: makkata, the monkey stuck in the pitch. Don't grab: pause before the second paw. Now, the last factor of the path.

Sunlight falling on a sheet of paper does nothing much. Gather the same sunlight through a magnifying glass, and the paper starts to smoke. Nothing was added. No extra sun. The light was only collected into one point. Water from a garden hose works the same way: spread into a mist, it barely wets the grass; gathered into a stream, it reaches the far end of the yard. The eighth and last factor of the eightfold path is about that kind of gathering.
screen: `THE SAME SUNLIGHT.` → `GATHERED INTO ONE POINT.` → `NOTHING ADDED.`

segments.voice: In Pali it's samma samadhi. Samadhi is usually explained from a verb meaning to put together, to collect: the mind gathered. In MN 141, where Sariputta lays out the four noble truths, right concentration is defined simply as the four jhanas, four deepening states of meditative absorption. The next four days take them one at a time, with the Buddha's own pictures. Today is about the gathering itself, and three things. First, it isn't a strain, not frowning hard at a point. In the suttas' pictures of the jhanas, the gathered mind is pleasant, even joyful. Second, it's never alone. MN 117 calls it noble right concentration with its supports: the seven factors that come before it. A mind gathered to plan a burglary is gathered, too. It isn't right concentration. Third, concentration and understanding work as partners. The Dhammapada says, in Max Müller's translation: “Without knowledge there is no meditation, without meditation there is no knowledge: he who has knowledge and meditation is near unto Nirvana.” Buddhist schools differ on how much concentration a person needs, and how deep. In Theravada teaching, calm, samatha, and insight, vipassana, are often described as developed together; some teachers stress deep absorption, others a lighter, moment-to-moment steadiness. Zen and Tibetan schools train the gathered mind in their own ways.
screen: `SAMADHI — THE MIND GATHERED.` · `NOT A STRAIN, AND NEVER ALONE.` · `KNOWLEDGE AND MEDITATION TOGETHER.` · `SCHOOLS DIFFER ON HOW DEEP.` · then, large: `GATHERED.`

segments.voice: Choose one place where the breath is clearest, the nostrils or the belly, and let your attention rest there; when it scatters, gather it back gently, the way you'd sweep crumbs into your hand. Every gathering is the practice, and if you have ten minutes today, this is a good day to use them.
Samadhi. Concentration: the mind gathered and unified, the eighth factor of the path.
Your line: gathered. Nothing added, only the same light collected into one point. See you tomorrow.

396.title: The first jhana
396.hook: like bath powder kneaded with water until it is soaked through: joy filling the body (MN 39)
396.howItsDone: Jhana practice is taught especially in Theravada meditation lineages, usually with a teacher and often on retreat; Chan and Zen take their names from the same word, dhyana.

segments.voice: Yesterday: samadhi, right concentration, the mind gathered like sunlight into one point.

A boy sits in the cool shade of a rose-apple tree while his father is busy with the work of the day. Nobody is watching him. And something happens: his mind goes quiet and bright, and his body fills with a gentle joy. Years later, after a long stretch of starving himself and pushing his body to its limit, that grown man remembers the afternoon under the tree, and wonders: could that be the way to awakening?
screen: `UNDER THE ROSE-APPLE TREE.` → `QUIET, BRIGHT, GLAD.` → `COULD THAT BE THE WAY?`

segments.voice: The man is the Buddha-to-be, and he tells this story himself, in MN 36. He'd been wary of that kind of pleasure, he says; then he saw he didn't need to fear it, because it had nothing to do with sense pleasures. Jhana is the Pali word. In Sanskrit it's dhyana, the same word that traveled to China as chan and to Japan as zen. It means meditative absorption. In MN 39 the Buddha describes the first one: quite secluded from sense pleasures and unwholesome states, a person enters the first jhana, with directed and sustained thought, and with joy and pleasure born of that seclusion. Then a picture from a world before bars of soap. A skilled bath attendant pours bath powder into a metal bowl, sprinkles it with water bit by bit, and kneads it into a ball, until the moisture soaks every grain, inside and out, yet doesn't drip. That's how this joy fills the body. It's physical: it drenches the whole body. It's thorough: no part is left dry. It's contained: nothing leaks. And there's still a hand at work: thinking is present, directed and sustained, like the attendant's hands working the powder. The later jhanas let even that settle. One honest note: teachers today disagree about how deep this state is. Some describe a rare, total absorption; others a calmer, more accessible steadiness. The texts give pictures, not a depth gauge.
screen: `JHANA, DHYANA, CHAN, ZEN.` · `SECLUDED, YET STILL THINKING.` · `BATH POWDER SOAKED THROUGH.` · `TEACHERS DIFFER ON HOW DEEP.` · then, large: `SOAKED THROUGH.`

segments.voice: No need to reach for joy; look for any ease already here, warm hands, shoulders letting go on the out-breath, a soft belly. Find one small place of ease and see whether it can spread, slowly, like water into powder, and if you find nothing, that's honest too: rest with the breath.
Jhana. Meditative absorption. In the first, joy born of seclusion soaks the whole body, like water kneaded into bath powder.
Your line: soaked through. Joy that fills the whole body and doesn't drip. That's day three hundred ninety-six.

397.title: The second jhana
397.hook: a lake fed by a spring from within (MN 39)
397.howItsDone: Meditators who train in the jhanas usually do so under a teacher's guidance, often on retreat; many Buddhists also use the phrase 'noble silence' for periods of silence kept at retreats.

segments.voice: Yesterday: jhana, and the first one: joy that soaks the body like water kneaded into bath powder.

Some lakes are filled by rivers: water pours down from the hills, and if the rivers dry up, the lake shrinks. Some are topped up by rain. And some are filled from beneath. A cold spring wells up from the lakebed, and the lake stays full even in a dry season. You can't see where the water is coming from. It just keeps arriving.
screen: `FED BY RIVERS.` → `FED BY RAIN.` → `FED FROM BENEATH.`

segments.voice: In MN 39 the Buddha describes the next stage. With the stilling of directed and sustained thought, a person enters the second jhana: inner confidence, the mind become one, without directed or sustained thought, with joy and pleasure born of concentration. Then his picture: a lake whose waters well up from below. No stream flows in from the east, the west, the north or the south. The sky doesn't fill it with rain from time to time. But a cool spring wells up within it and soaks the whole lake, so that no part is left untouched. Set it beside yesterday's picture. In the first jhana, water was added by a hand, sprinkled and kneaded into the powder, and the joy was born of seclusion, of stepping away. Here the hand is gone. Thinking has gone quiet, and the joy is born of concentration itself; it rises from inside. Two Pali words carry this. Sampasadana: inner clearness, or inner confidence; one way to picture it is muddy water settling until you can see the bottom. And ekodibhava: the mind becoming single, unified. The calm doesn't depend on anything outside: no good news, no compliment, no perfect weather. In SN 21.1, Moggallana tells how he came to see that the second jhana is what's called noble silence. Not the silence of a closed mouth, but of a mind that has stopped talking to itself.
screen: `THINKING GROWS STILL.` · `A LAKE FED FROM WITHIN.` · `NO RIVER, NO RAIN.` · `NOBLE SILENCE.` · then, large: `THE INNER SPRING.`

segments.voice: Let the breath settle, and when a thought comes, let it pass without picking it up. Between thoughts there may be small gaps, a breath or two with nothing to do; rest in one and notice whether anything wells up on its own, quiet, coolness, a little gladness, and if nothing does, the gap itself is enough.
Sampasadana, inner clearness. Thinking grows still, and joy wells up from within, like a lake fed by its own spring.
Your line: the inner spring. A calm that depends on nothing outside, welling up from within. Until tomorrow.

398.title: The third jhana
398.hook: lotuses under water, soaked from root to tip (MN 39)
398.howItsDone: In Theravada meditation teaching the jhanas are usually described in this order, with the fading of rapture and the growth of equanimity marking the third; the lotus is a common Buddhist image in art and teaching across schools.

segments.voice: Yesterday: sampasadana, inner clearness, the lake fed by its own spring. The inner spring.

In a lotus pond, most of the flowers rise up and open on the surface, where everyone can see them. Those are the ones on the postcards. But some never come up. They sprout under water, grow under water, and stay there, cool water all around them from the roots to the tips of the petals. You'd walk right past them. Nothing about them is showy. They're thriving anyway.

Here is how MN 39 describes the third jhana. With the fading away of joy, a person abides in equanimity, mindful and fully aware, still feeling pleasure with the body, and enters the third jhana, of which the noble ones say: one who is equanimous and mindful dwells in pleasure. Then the picture. In a pond of blue, red or white lotuses, some are born and grow in the water and thrive immersed, never rising out, and cool water soaks them from their tips to their roots. That's how this quiet pleasure fills the body. What changes from yesterday? Two Pali words help. Piti is joy with a bubble in it: rapture, excitement, the child on the morning of a trip. Sukha is pleasure without the bubble: contentment, the grandmother on the porch. In the third jhana, piti fades and sukha stays, and a new quality comes forward: upekkha, equanimity, looking on evenly. Many centuries later, the Visuddhimagga, a Theravada meditation manual, gives an image for the difference. A traveler worn out in the desert hears that there's a pond at the edge of a wood: that thrill is piti. Then he reaches it, drinks and rests in the shade: that's sukha. The third jhana is happiness that no longer needs to rise and be seen; the mind stays mindful and fully aware, and the ease simply soaks through.
screen: `THE JOY FADES; THE EASE STAYS.` · `PITI, BUBBLING; SUKHA, CONTENT.` · `HEARING OF WATER, THEN DRINKING.` · `LOTUSES SOAKED, ROOT TO TIP.` · then, large: `THE LOTUS UNDER WATER.`

segments.voice: Don't look for anything bright; let the breath be ordinary, and notice whether there's any plain, quiet okayness in the body, not excitement, just enough. If thoughts come, let them pass like ripples on the surface overhead, while you stay below, cool and still.
Upekkha, equanimity. The bubbling joy fades and a quiet, mindful ease remains, like a lotus soaked in cool water from root to tip.
Your line: the lotus under water. Thriving, with nothing showy about it. Day three hundred ninety-eight, done.

399.title: The fourth jhana
399.hook: a person wrapped head to foot in clean white cloth (MN 39)
399.howItsDone: In Theravada teaching the fourth jhana is often described as the basis for insight and the higher knowledges; meditators who work with the jhanas usually do so under a teacher; the suttas tell both the Buddha's awakening and his final passing with the fourth jhana.

segments.voice: Yesterday: upekkha, equanimity, and the lotus that thrives under water. Your line: the lotus under water. Today, the last of the four pictures, and the end of the week.

A clean white cloth, fresh off the line, still cool. Someone sits down, and the cloth is drawn over them from the top of the head to the soles of the feet. Not to hide them. Just to cover them evenly, all the way around. No part warmer than another. No part left out. Almost nothing happens in this picture, and that's the point. It's the last of the Buddha's four pictures of deep concentration.
screen: `A CLEAN WHITE CLOTH.` → `HEAD TO FOOT, EVENLY.` → `NOTHING LEFT OUT.`

segments.voice: MN 39 describes it this way. Pleasure and pain are both let go, as gladness and sorrow faded earlier. What's left is neither painful nor pleasant: mindfulness made pure by equanimity. A person sits pervading the body with a pure, bright mind, like someone wrapped from the head down in white cloth, so that no part of the body is uncovered. Look at the path the four jhanas trace. First, thinking settles. Then the bubbling joy fades. Now even pleasure is let go. Each stage is less, not more, and what's left is plain as the cloth: no pattern, no color, nothing to grab. Strangely, the suttas treat this not as an ending but as a platform. In MN 36, the Buddha says that on the night of his awakening, his mind concentrated like this, pure and bright, steady and pliable, he directed it toward knowledge, and the three knowledges followed. And in DN 16, the Great Discourse on the Final Nibbana, his last moments pass through the jhanas, and he passes away on emerging from the fourth. So the week ends here: the quail on its own ground, the monkey and the pitch, then right concentration in four pictures. Bath powder soaked through, a lake fed by a spring, lotuses under water, a person wrapped in white. Each quieter than the last.
screen: `PLEASURE AND PAIN BOTH LET GO.` · `PURE MINDFULNESS, EQUANIMITY.` · `WRAPPED HEAD TO FOOT IN WHITE.` · `A PLATFORM FOR KNOWING.` · then, large: `WRAPPED IN WHITE.`

segments.voice: Let your attention cover the body evenly, head to foot, the way the cloth covers, with no spot more interesting than another. If something itches, it can itch; if something is pleasant, it can be pleasant, with no chasing and no pushing away. Rest in the middle, and let it all be covered by plain, clear knowing.
Fourth jhana. The last of the four deep meditative absorptions: neither pleasure nor pain, only equanimity and mindfulness, like a body wrapped evenly in white cloth.
Your line: wrapped in white. In the suttas, this stillness is where seeing begins. Go gently.

fork.setup: your mind is still, pure and bright, covered by equanimity like a white cloth. in MN 36, what does the Buddha-to-be do next?
options: stays there as long as possible
directs the clear mind toward knowledge
gets up and goes to find food
fork.reveal: he directed it toward knowledge, and the three knowledges of the night of awakening followed. the stillness was a platform, not the destination.

original.note: Pali upekkhā-sati-pārisuddhi: purity of mindfulness through equanimity, the mark of the fourth jhāna.

trapdoor: what you thought: the deepest jhana must be the most blissful.
what it means: even pleasure is let go, leaving equanimity and pure mindfulness, even as a white cloth.
what a scholar hears: the stock phrase upekkhā-sati-pārisuddhi, purity of mindfulness through equanimity; in DN 16 the Buddha's final passing follows his emerging from the fourth jhāna.
recall: a lute: effort tuned to an even pitch

chat.says: Isn't the deepest meditation just the most blissful feeling you can get?
options: Even pleasure is let go there; what's left is equanimity and clear mindfulness.
Yes, each jhana adds more bliss, and the fourth is the peak of pleasure.
No, the fourth jhana is a blank trance where awareness switches off.
chat.meaning: MN 39 describes the fourth jhana as neither painful nor pleasant, with mindfulness made pure by equanimity.

Nibbana.meaning: release, the end of suffering; here, the Buddha's final passing
